title: Trading page scripts for CSS changes keyboards more than bytes
description: Five PRs swapped page scripts for HTML and CSS. Measured in three engines for pixels, bytes, work per press, keyboard and the XP look.
bodyHtml:
Trading page scripts for CSS changes keyboards more than bytes

Aleth Gueguen's Go fast? Go web native at performance.now() 2026 closes on a question it leaves open: can the JavaScript behind an interactive element give way to modern HTML? Five stacked PRs here tried it on 22 pages, under one claim: functionally identical. This page measures that claim in Chromium 158, Firefox 159 and WebKit 27.2. It checks pixels at load and after every press, bytes on the wire, work per press, the keyboard, and how the browser's own controls sit next to Luna.

Five PRs, 32.8 KB of script, +2,055 bytes on the wire

PRwhat it convertspagesinline scriptsinline script, rawdocuments, compressed

1893/lens: invokers, details, forms10 to 00.0 KB to 0.0 KB19.6 KB to 19.7 KB +129 B

The stack takes 164.6 KB of inline script on these pages down to 131.8 KB. 7 pages now ship no inline script at all, so the Worker sends them its strictest script-src. The documents a visitor downloads barely move, because brotli had already squeezed the script into a few hundred bytes and the markup that replaces it compresses just as well. PR 1891 removes 28.7 KB of raw script and its pages shrink by 254 B in total. /restore grows by 2,211 B, since each of its 131 restore points now ships a preformatted date.

So bytes are not the argument for this. What changes is behaviour, and that is what the rest of the page measures.

Most of the site has to stay script

Before the stack, three read-only passes sorted every client script by what it needs. A script goes when HTML or CSS does its whole job, goes in part when a piece of it does, and stays when it needs something only script has.

wherereadcan go wholecan go in partstays script

Garage page scripts4171321
LWE, home, /access, Pixel Peeper244416
read first, by hand8314
every page script73141841

What stays has one shape: tooltips that follow the cursor, fetched JSON, timers, storage, drag math, canvas and WebGL, Web Audio, hashing, and arithmetic on free text or a slider with 40,401 positions. CSS can't read a range input's value, hold a timer or open a socket. The shell kept about 97 percent of its lines for those reasons.

About Notepad

This is a real text field: edit it however you like. Nothing saves, so a reload restores my canonical version. The writing here is always in flux.

Pixels decide what counts as identical

Each page loads three times: twice from the commit the PR sits on and once from the PR. Playwright screenshots all three, then presses every button, radio, checkbox and summary the old page offers, in both, and screenshots the section around it. A state counts as identical only when every RGB value matches. The two loads of the old page are the control. A page that differs from itself, like the homepage's now-playing track or masonry's shuffled photos, reads "changes on reload" and is judged by its text alone.

What the oracle caught

  • gpt56 shows all three readouts at once. PR 1891 hides the unpicked readouts with .sol-ro{display:none} and then, later in the same sheet, gives every readout .readouts{display:grid}. Same specificity, later rule wins, so the "bytes" and "ship" numbers sit under the meter from first paint.
  • hidden-flags stripes unevenly when filtered. The script rebuilt the table on every click, so :nth-child(odd) striped the rows you could see. CSS that hides rows keeps them in the count. :nth-child(odd of [data-g=config]) stripes among the rows a filter keeps, which is what the HTML twin above does. The PR also adds about 15 px of space under the demo.
  • tee keeps the picked attack pressed. The buttons used to spring back; the radios stay down. That one reads as an improvement.
  • fuse's first demo works again. On the commit the stack starts from, pressing "flash this build" throws e.appendChild is not a function. The build minifies inline scripts under a filename with no .js extension, so Oxc parses them as strict modules. In a module, a function declared inside an if block belongs to that block, so the mangler reuses its name. The browser runs the script in sloppy mode, where that function also lands in the enclosing scope, and the two names collide. PR 1891 fixes fuse by accident, since its rewrite drops the block. 9 of 72 inline scripts minify differently once the filename ends in .js.
  • gpt56 keeps its glossary link. The old script rewrote the copy with textContent, so "preload" lost its link after one round trip, and the meter loaded at 68 percent where its data said 74. One radio state per panel removes both.

The bench twins went through this site's own build steps: Oxc for script, Lightning CSS for styles, the HTML minifier, then brotli at quality 11 over the whole page.

The dialog saves the most, 264 B, because its markup was already sitting in a string inside the script. The filter grows: 19 rows and eight count lines written out cost 48 B more than the loop that built them. The sibling twins cost more again, because without :has() each label needs its own pressed-state rule.

Time is a tie until the table gets long

Two instruments timed each press. The first runs from the click to a task queued behind the next animation frame, which is what a reader waits for. The second times the work alone: script, style and layout, forced by reading offsetHeight straight after the click. The fixtures were served cross-origin isolated, so performance.now() resolves below a millisecond in all three engines.

The control is the JS tabs twin with a 20 ms busy-wait in its handler. The work instrument reads it as 20.45 ms in Chromium. The paint instrument reads the same 20 ms as only 5.7 ms more, because a click that finishes early still waits for the next frame. So the table below reports work.

At 4,750 rows the :has() twin does 3.1x the JS twin's work in Chromium, 2.5x in Firefox and 10.7x in WebKit. The sibling twin hides the same rows with #hf-config:checked ~ .hf-scroll tr and no :has(). It lands at 1.4x of JS in Chromium and 1.1x in Firefox, so in those engines most of the cost is :has(). Every row's rules ask a question about an ancestor, and flipping a radio inside that ancestor makes the engine ask again for all 4,750 rows. WebKit is slow without it too, at 2.9x for the sibling twin, so there restyling thousands of rows costs more than rebuilding the few the script keeps.

Skipping the offscreen rows

Two more variants of the 4,750-row twins tried to stop the browser styling rows nobody can see. content-visibility: auto asks the engine to skip an offscreen element's contents. Grid rows with fixed columns make each row size itself, so a skipped row never feeds a column width the whole table shares. The last column asks a cell in the last row whether its row was skipped, with checkVisibility({ contentVisibilityAuto: true }).

On a table, content-visibility does nothing in any engine: a table row is an internal table box, size containment has no effect on one, and the cells report themselves rendered. Grid rows on their own change nothing either. Together they skip the offscreen rows in all three engines and cut the JS twin's work in Chromium from 26.81 ms to 4.26 ms, and the sibling twin's from 30.14 ms to 10.7 ms. The :has() twin halves in Chromium and gains nothing in WebKit, where it stays above a second. The price is the table itself: fixed columns no longer size to their content, so the grid version is a different layout, which the pixel oracle would flag.

Putting the sibling twin's radios back inside a fieldset that wraps the whole demo costs nothing measurable in Chromium and Firefox: at 4,750 rows, 28.85 ms against 29.54 ms in Chromium and 34.96 ms against 34.92 ms in Firefox. WebKit read 543.56 ms against 292.98 ms, a gap from 3 loads and 24 presses that I haven't explained.

Radios change four things a keyboard user meets. In Chromium and Firefox the JS tabs are 3 Tab stops and the JS filter is 8; each radio group is 1, and the arrow keys move the pick. Enter picks a button and does nothing on a radio. Firefox restores a checked radio on reload, where every JS twin starts over; autocomplete="off" on the inputs keeps the old behaviour. And the accessibility tree reads radio [checked] where it read button [pressed]. PR 1891 makes that trade on eight pages and its body doesn't mention it. gpt56 also loses the aria-live that announced each new readout.

WebKit, like Safari by default, sends Tab past buttons and radios alike, so there both twins are reached the same way, with Option-Tab. The plain sibling twin has a cost the others don't. Its radios sit before the table so ~ can reach it, which puts them outside the fieldset that names them, and a screen reader hears eight radios with no group. The third twin on the bench wraps the whole demo in the fieldset and gets the name back.

Native controls next to Luna

PR 1892 hands several controls to the browser. The question for this site is whether they still look like Windows XP. Each surface below was captured from the commit the PR sits on and from the PR, in all three engines.

The validation bubble is the one no stylesheet can fix, because the browser draws it outside the page. This site already has an XP balloon (#axp-balloon). Keeping the <form> and its implicit submit, and showing the length rule in that balloon, keeps the native wiring and the Luna look.

The script has states the markup doesn't

Stéphanie Walter's Performance, As a Design Opportunity asks a team to design each state a component can be in: loading, taking longer, error, empty. Run her checklist on a JS twin and it has two states nobody designed. Before its script runs, the hidden-flags filter is an empty bar over an empty table. If the script fails, it stays that way, which is what fuse's first demo did for every visitor until the stack. With JavaScript turned off, the JS filter showed 0 rows and 0 filters in all three engines, and every CSS filter showed all 19 rows with 8 working filters.

What each PR needs before it merges

  • 1889 merges as is. typed-config now keeps its 13 bindings twice, in the table and in the picker's array, so one should derive the other.
  • 1890 merges for scroll, safari27 and pixel-peeper. Masonry leaves its masonry radio checked and reachable on browsers without grid-lanes, which is Safari 26 and Firefox, while the page shows fixed squares; the old code disabled the button.
  • 1891 needs the gpt56 readout rule reordered, the hidden-flags stripes moved to :nth-child(odd of S), gpt56's aria-live back, and a body that names the keyboard change on eight pages.
  • 1892 needs a Tab stop for the chunks drop zone in Safari and an XP balloon in place of the native validation bubble. The grip, the note close box and the /access tree hold the look.
  • 1893 needs /lens* excluded from the site's speculation rules. Its chips are now real links, and hovering one would prerender /lens?url=, which runs a full server-side inspection of a third-party site.

The trade is worth making where a page has a small, fixed set of states: it removes code that can break, as fuse did, and the demos keep working without JavaScript. It is a different control, though, and a pixel oracle is how you find out which parts of "identical" held.

editorial.reader: Someone who builds a site of small interactive demos and is weighing whether to replace its page scripts with modern HTML and CSS.
editorial.problem: Talks sell the swap on speed and bytes, and a PR calls it functionally identical, but nobody measures what changes for a keyboard, a screen reader, or the look when the browser draws the control.
editorial.thesis: On a site that already serves brotli, swapping page scripts for HTML and CSS barely moves bytes; it changes keyboard behaviour, adds no-JS behaviour, and needs a pixel oracle to catch what it breaks.
evidence: Five PRs remove 32.8 KB of inline script from 22 pages and move compressed documents by +2,055 B.
Screenshots at load and after every press, in three engines, caught a readout shown three times, uneven stripes, a drop zone Safari can't reach with Tab, and a live minifier bug.
Twins measured for work per press tie at 19 rows; at 4,750 rows :has() costs 3 to 11 times the script.
editorial.uncertainty: No screen reader was run: accessibility claims come from the accessibility tree. The /lens prerender cost is read from the code, because Chrome won't prerender with a debugger attached.

understanding.intro: Four questions on what an identical swap actually changed.

questions.q: PR 1891 removed 28.7 KB of inline script. Why did its pages shrink by only 254 B on the wire?

options.t: Brotli had already compressed the script to a few hundred bytes, and the markup that replaced it compresses as well.
options.why: Right. Raw script length is the wrong unit on a site that serves brotli; what a visitor downloads is the compressed document, and both versions compress well.

options.t: The browser cached the old inline scripts after the first visit, so removing them saves bytes only on a visitor's very first load of each page.
options.why: These are inline scripts, part of the document itself. The comparison is between two documents fetched fresh, so caching plays no part.

options.t: The scripts were deferred, so their bytes never counted toward the document the browser downloads.
options.why: Deferring changes when a script runs, never whether its bytes arrive. Inline script travels inside the HTML either way.

questions.q: After the conversion, the hidden-flags filter striped its rows unevenly. What changed?

options.t: Rows hidden with display:none still count for :nth-child, while the script used to rebuild only the rows you could see.
options.why: Right. The fix is :nth-child(odd of S), which counts only the rows matching the selector a filter keeps.

options.t: Picking a radio reset the zebra colours to the browser's default table styling, which alternates from the first row of the tbody instead of using the page's rule.
options.why: Picking a radio changes which rows are hidden. The stripe colours come from the page CSS and never reset.

options.t: Lightning CSS rewrote :nth-child(odd) into a selector that no longer matches a table row inside a tbody.
options.why: The minified rule still matches; the stripes land on the wrong rows because the hidden rows are still counted.

questions.q: gpt56 showed all three readouts at once after PR 1891. Why did the rule that hides them lose?

options.t: A later .readouts{display:grid} rule had the same specificity as .sol-ro{display:none}, so source order decided.
options.why: Right. With equal specificity the later declaration wins, and the :has() rule that shows the picked readout never had to fight anything.

options.t: The :has() rule that shows the picked readout matched all three, because every radio in a group counts as checked until the page finishes loading.
options.why: Only one radio in a group can be checked. The extra readouts show because the hide rule lost, so nothing hid them to begin with.

options.t: Chrome doesn't apply display:none to an element that is also a grid container, so the rule was skipped.
options.why: display:none applies to any element. It lost a cascade fight with a later rule of equal weight.

questions.q: Why can't CSS make the ask bar's minlength message look like Windows XP?

options.t: The browser draws the validation bubble outside the page, where no stylesheet on the page reaches it.
options.why: Right. Only the page's own balloon, fed the same rule, can carry the Luna look.

options.t: The bubble is drawn inside a closed shadow root on the input, and Luna's selectors stop at that boundary like every other page stylesheet's do.
options.why: There's no shadow root to pierce: the bubble is browser chrome drawn outside the page entirely.

options.t: Luna styles inputs by class, and the bubble is attached to the form element that holds them.
options.why: Where it attaches doesn't matter. The bubble is drawn by the browser outside the page, so page CSS never reaches it.
